## Statement of Need

Eastside County faces a literacy crisis that is measurable, persistent, and consequential for residents across generations. According to the State Department of Education (2023), 18% of Eastside County adults are functionally illiterate — a rate 50% higher than the state average of 12%. That gap represents thousands of residents who struggle to read a prescription label, complete a job application, or help a child with homework. Without targeted intervention, the data suggest this gap will not close on its own.

The impact begins early. The Eastside County School District (2022) found that 40% of local third graders are reading below grade level — a benchmark researchers consistently identify as a turning point, because students who are not reading proficiently by third grade are four times less likely to graduate high school on time. In Eastside County, that means roughly four in ten children enter their middle school years already behind. The connection between childhood and adult literacy is well established: children whose parents read proficiently at home develop literacy skills faster and are more likely to meet grade-level benchmarks themselves. Low adult literacy does not stay with adults alone — it moves forward through families.

The economic consequences are equally clear. A 2023 workforce survey conducted across Eastside County employers ranked "basic reading and digital literacy" as the single greatest barrier to entry-level employment, cited more frequently than transportation, childcare, or prior criminal history. Residents face this barrier daily. At intake, BrightPath learners regularly describe situations that reflect what the data show: being passed over for promotions because they could not complete required paperwork, avoiding the doctor because medical forms felt impossible to navigate, or feeling unable to advocate for their children at school. These are not isolated experiences — they are patterns rooted in a systemic gap between community need and available service.

That gap is not filled by existing providers. Eastside County currently has no public adult education program operating at the scale the population requires. The public library offers limited drop-in literacy support two days per week, with no structured curriculum and no case management. The nearest community college's adult basic education program serves fewer than 100 learners per year and maintains its own waitlist. BrightPath is the only community-based organization in the county providing structured, one-on-one adult literacy tutoring with wraparound coordination — and demand has outpaced our capacity.

BrightPath currently serves 350 adult learners annually. As of this application, 120 additional residents are on our waitlist, with an average wait time of six months. For someone who needs literacy skills to pursue a job, support a child's education, or manage a health condition, six months is not a minor inconvenience — it is a semester of school their child finishes without them, a job opportunity that will not wait, a prescription that goes misread. The waitlist is not a number; it is a measure of unmet need in real time.

Eastside County's literacy gap is wider than the state's, growing faster than local services can address it, and carrying consequences that compound across generations. The residents who come to BrightPath are not asking for something extraordinary — they are asking for the foundational skills that most people take for granted. The question this grant asks the funder to answer is straightforward: how many more residents should wait before they get that chance?

## Target Population

BrightPath's target population is adult residents of Eastside County who read below a sixth-grade level, with priority given to those facing compounding barriers: unemployment or underemployment, limited English proficiency, or children currently enrolled in the county's K–12 system. To be eligible, participants must be 18 years of age or older, reside in Eastside County, and demonstrate literacy need through an intake assessment using the TABE (Tests of Adult Basic Education), a nationally normed tool administered by trained BrightPath staff during the enrollment appointment. Residency is verified through a utility bill, lease, or government-issued ID. No participant is turned away based on immigration status or prior education history.

The population we serve reflects the county's demographics and its inequities. Approximately 62% of current learners are women; the median age is 38. Roughly 55% identify as Hispanic or Latino, 22% as Black or African American, and 18% as white — a demographic profile consistent with state and national patterns showing that literacy gaps fall disproportionately along lines of race and historical access to quality schooling. Nearly 90% of enrolled participants fall at or below 200% of the federal poverty level, and 67% are either unemployed or working part-time in jobs below their stated career goals.

BrightPath serves 350 adult learners per year. Over a two-year grant period, we project serving 700 unduplicated individuals, drawing from our current waitlist of 120 and an estimated 230 new referrals annually from workforce development partners, the county health department, and school family liaisons.

This population is underserved not for lack of motivation — our waitlist proves demand — but because no other provider in Eastside County offers structured, individualized adult literacy instruction at scale. These residents have fallen outside every system designed to help them, and they are asking for one more chance to get in.

## Program Design & Activities

**Theory of Change**

BrightPath operates from a straightforward theory of change: when adults with low literacy receive structured, individualized instruction delivered at sufficient dosage over a sustained period, paired with goal-aligned support services, they gain measurable literacy skills that translate into improved employment outcomes, greater capacity to support their children's education, and stronger long-term self-sufficiency. The logic model attached as Figure 1 maps inputs, activities, outputs, and outcomes in full. The narrative below describes how that logic works in practice.

**Core Activities**

BrightPath's program model is built on three mutually reinforcing core activities: individualized literacy instruction, digital literacy and workforce readiness training, and family engagement support. Together they address the layered barriers Eastside County residents face — not just reading skill, but the applied contexts in which that skill must function.

*Activity 1: Individualized Literacy Instruction*

The foundation of BrightPath's model is one-on-one tutoring delivered by trained volunteer tutors and supervised by a certified literacy specialist. Each participant is matched with a tutor within two weeks of completing intake and begins a personalized learning plan based on their TABE assessment results and stated goals. Sessions meet twice weekly for 90 minutes each, yielding a weekly dosage of three hours of direct instruction — consistent with the dosage threshold identified in research on adult literacy program effectiveness (Kruidenier, MacArthur & Woo, 2010). Participants remain in active tutoring for a minimum of six months, with an option to continue for a second six-month term based on progress and goals.

Each cohort enrolls 35 participants and launches on a rolling quarterly basis, yielding four cohorts per year and a total active enrollment of up to 140 participants at any given time. Across the full year, with cohort cycling and re-enrollment, BrightPath serves 350 unduplicated adult learners. Instruction takes place at BrightPath's Eastside County Learning Center and at two satellite locations — a branch library and a community health clinic — chosen specifically to reduce transportation barriers for participants in the county's lower-income eastern and southern neighborhoods.

This activity directly addresses the literacy gap documented in the Statement of Need and links to Outcome 1: participants demonstrating measurable gains on post-program TABE assessment.

*Activity 2: Digital Literacy and Workforce Readiness Training*

Recognizing that the 2023 Eastside County workforce survey identified "basic reading and digital literacy" as the top barrier to employment, BrightPath integrates a six-week digital literacy module into every participant's second month of enrollment. Delivered in small groups of eight to ten participants by BrightPath's Workforce Readiness Coordinator, sessions cover email and internet basics, navigating online job applications, and using digital tools for household and health management. The module draws on the Northstar Digital Literacy framework, which has demonstrated effectiveness across diverse adult learner populations in community-based settings (Digital Literacy Alliance, 2021).

One participant, now employed full-time after completing the program, described the shift this way: she had always avoided applying for certain jobs because the online application felt like a wall she couldn't get past. Learning to navigate that process was, she said, the moment things started to open up. Her experience reflects what the data consistently show — that literacy gains translate into employment outcomes only when participants also have practice applying those skills in real-world digital contexts.

This activity links to Outcome 2: participants reporting increased confidence in digital navigation and demonstrating improved workforce readiness competencies.

*Activity 3: Family Engagement Support*

Because 40% of Eastside County third graders read below grade level, and because parental literacy is one of the strongest predictors of children's reading development, BrightPath offers monthly family literacy workshops for participants who have children in grades K–5. Workshops, capped at 20 families, are facilitated by the Family Engagement Coordinator and focus on shared reading strategies, library use, and how to support homework without formal tutoring. Research consistently links structured family literacy programming to improvements in both adult learner persistence and children's reading outcomes (Wasik & Hendrickson, 2004). A father enrolled in the program last year put it plainly: he came for himself, but staying was about his daughter — once he could read with her at night, she stopped dreading school.

This activity links to Outcome 3: participants reporting increased engagement in their children's literacy development, and to the intergenerational dimension of the community impact criteria.

**Participant Pathway**

Participants move through four clearly defined phases. During intake, prospective learners contact BrightPath by phone, referral, or walk-in; complete an eligibility screening; and are scheduled for a TABE assessment within five business days. During matching and orientation, assessed participants are matched with a tutor, receive a one-hour program orientation, and co-develop their learning plan with staff. Active services then begin, running for a minimum of six months as described above, with monthly check-ins between the participant, tutor, and literacy specialist to review progress and adjust the plan. At exit, participants complete a post-program TABE assessment, receive a transition plan outlining next steps — workforce programs, community college, continued independent learning — and are scheduled for a 90-day follow-up contact to track employment and continued progress outcomes.

Together they demonstrate that BrightPath has the personnel and sequencing in place to launch the first cohort within 60 days of a funding award.

## Section 6: Outcomes & Objectives

BrightPath's outcomes framework distinguishes clearly between outputs — the services we deliver — and outcomes — the changes participants experience as a result. The four SMART objectives below are anchored to local baselines established in our Statement of Need and tracked across both years of the grant period. Annual targets are set conservatively in year one to account for start-up and ramp-up, with higher targets in year two reflecting full operational capacity.

**Objective 1: Literacy Skill Gains**
By the end of year one, 75% of participants who complete a minimum of six months of individualized literacy instruction (at least 70% attendance) will demonstrate a measurable gain of one or more grade levels on the TABE post-assessment, compared to their baseline score at intake. By the end of year two, that rate will reach 80%. This objective responds directly to the county's adult functional illiteracy rate of 18% (State Department of Education, 2023) and establishes literacy skill gain as the program's primary participant-level outcome.

**Objective 2: Digital Literacy and Workforce Readiness**
By the end of year one, 70% of participants completing the six-week digital literacy module will demonstrate proficiency on at least three of five Northstar Digital Literacy competency areas assessed at module completion, up from an estimated baseline of fewer than 30% at intake. By the end of year two, that rate will reach 75%. This objective is grounded in the 2023 Eastside County workforce survey finding that basic digital literacy is the top barrier to local employment, and links directly to Objective 3.

**Objective 3: Employment Outcomes**
By the end of year one, 40% of participants who exit the program having met their literacy and digital literacy goals will report obtaining or retaining employment, or advancing to a higher-wage position, within 90 days of exit, verified through participant self-report and, where possible, employer confirmation. By the end of year two, that rate will reach 50%. Baseline for this measure is established at intake through employment status documentation; 67% of enrolled participants currently enter the program unemployed or underemployed.

**Objective 4: Family Literacy Engagement**
By the end of year one, 80% of participants with children in grades K–5 who attend at least three of six family literacy workshops will report increased confidence in supporting their child's reading at home, as measured by a pre/post participant survey administered by BrightPath staff. By the end of year two, 80% will be maintained as the target, with an added secondary indicator: a 5-percentage-point improvement in third-grade reading proficiency among children of enrolled participants, tracked in coordination with the County School District. This objective addresses the county's 40% third-grade below-grade-level rate (County School District, 2022) and captures the program's intergenerational impact.

A summary output target runs beneath all four objectives: BrightPath will serve 350 unduplicated adult learners in year one and 350 in year two, for a total of 700 individuals over the grant period, reducing the current waitlist of 120 by at least 50% by the end of year one through expanded intake capacity.

## Section 7: Evaluation Plan

BrightPath's evaluation plan is designed to answer three questions continuously across the grant period: Are we reaching the right people? Are participants making meaningful gains? And are we using what we learn to get better? The plan uses a pre/post design with benchmark comparisons, mixed data collection methods, and a structured continuous improvement cycle.

**Evaluation Design**

BrightPath will use a pre/post design with a quasi-experimental benchmark comparison as its primary evaluation approach. Each participant serves as their own control, with TABE scores, Northstar competency assessments, employment status, and survey responses collected at intake (baseline), at the program midpoint (three months), at exit (six months), and at 90-day follow-up. Outcome rates will be benchmarked against published national averages for community-based adult literacy programs — specifically the most recent ProLiteracy national program data and the National Reporting System for Adult Education — to contextualize BrightPath's results within the broader field. While a randomized control design is not feasible in a community-based setting serving a waitlisted population, the pre/post structure with external benchmarking provides a credible and transparent basis for outcome claims.

**Data Collection Tools and Frequency**

TABE assessments are administered at intake and exit by the Certified Literacy Specialist, who holds the required certification for standardized administration. Northstar Digital Literacy competency checks are administered by the Workforce Readiness Coordinator at the start and end of the six-week module. Attendance is recorded by volunteer tutors at every session and entered into BrightPath's participant database by the Administrative Assistant within 48 hours. Employment status is documented at intake through participant self-report and verified at 90-day follow-up through a structured phone or in-person contact conducted by the Program Director or a designated staff member. Family engagement outcomes are measured through a brief pre/post survey, developed internally and reviewed annually, administered by the Family Engagement Coordinator at the first and last workshop of each cohort cycle.

**Data Management, Analysis, and Privacy**

All participant data are stored in BrightPath's secure case management database, accessible only to authorized staff and protected by password authentication and role-based permissions. No participant data are shared externally in identifiable form. Aggregate, de-identified data are used for all reporting, presentations, and publications. The Program Director conducts a quarterly data review, pulling outcome rates by cohort, attendance trends, and assessment completion rates, and presents findings to the Executive Director and Board Program Committee at each quarterly meeting.

**Continuous Improvement**

Findings from quarterly reviews feed directly into program adjustments through a structured continuous improvement protocol. If cohort-level TABE gain rates fall below 70% at the midpoint review, the Certified Literacy Specialist conducts individual plan reviews with the relevant tutors and participants within 30 days. If Northstar completion rates fall below target, the Workforce Readiness Coordinator reviews module pacing and delivery format. Staff reflect collectively on outcome trends at a annual program retreat each January, producing a written improvement plan that is shared with the Board and incorporated into the following year's work plan. Findings are also shared with key community partners — the County School District, workforce development partners, and the county health department — annually, both to strengthen referral relationships and to contribute to the broader evidence base for literacy programming in Eastside County.

**Reporting**

BrightPath will provide the funder with a midyear progress report at month six of each grant year, including output data, preliminary outcome rates, and a brief narrative on any program adjustments made. A full annual report will be submitted within 60 days of each grant year's close, including final outcome data against all four SMART objectives, a budget variance explanation, and a forward-looking narrative describing plans for year two (or sustainability, in the final year report).
